title: HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching

paper.title: HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching
paper.abstract: Abstract Individual-level genotype data underpin genetic discovery, disease-risk modeling, and therapeutic development, yet many critical settings remain data-limited, including underrepresented ancestries, rare or imbalanced disease cohorts, and restricted-access biobanks. Conditional synthetic genome generation would support privacy-aware benchmarking, simulation, and data augmentation, but requires learning an ultra-high-dimensional discrete distribution over hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of correlated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), or sites of DNA variation. We introduce HELICS : H igh-fidelity g E neration via L atent I nterpolant C onditional S ynthesis, a phasing-free latent flow matching framework for genome-wide SNP-level generation from biobank-scale genotype data. HELICS tokenizes chromosomes with convolutional autoencoders, reducing > > 600 ​ K 600{\rm K} SNPs to 4,096 4{,}096 continuous latent tokens, and trains a transformer parameterized conditional flow matching model over the concatenated multi-chromosome latent representation. Trained on over 417 ​ K 417\rm K genomes in the UK Biobank, HELICS generates genome-wide common-variant synthetic cohorts without haplotype phasing and achieves stronger fidelity to held-out real genotypes than existing haplotype- and genotype-based simulators, including high allele-frequency agreement in external evaluation ( R 2 = 0.992 R^{2}=0.992 ) and superior preservation of local and long-range SNP correlation structure. Conditioning on ancestry and genetic liability summaries enables targeted generation across genetic risk profiles; in perturbation analyses, by increasing the conditioned disease trait liability, HELICS induces SNP-level dosage changes in generated genomes that are highly correlated with published association weights. HELICS provides a scalable generative modeling framework for SNP-level genome data and a path toward conditional synthetic cohorts for data-limited genetic studies.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Modern genetic studies increasingly depend on large cohorts of individual-level genotype data, motivating major investments in biobanks for genome-wide association studies (GWAS), polygenic risk modeling, and therapeutic target discovery. However, collecting genotype data at the scale needed to answer crucial scientific questions remains slow and costly. Existing cohorts are highly imbalanced across ancestries, biasing discovery toward well-represented populations; many diseases are rare and have small sample sizes; and individual-level data are sensitive, identifiable, and access-controlled. These common data-scarce settings motivate synthetic genome generation not only as a privacy mechanism, but importantly, as a way to construct realistic, controllable genotypes to support method development, fairer and more powerful analyses of underrepresented ancestries, and even discovery of genetic mechanisms relevant to disease and therapeutic development. Rather than modeling the four-letter DNA sequence directly, population-scale genetic analyses typically focus on specific sites of genomic variation known as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). SNPs are the primary coordinates used to link genetic differences across individuals to disease risk, complex traits, and population history [ 1 , 55 , 3 , 39 ] . Many genetic analyses focus on common variants (observed in >1% of the population) as they are well-powered for association testing and capture substantial polygenic variation. SNPs are represented as dosage vectors 𝑮 ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } L \boldsymbol{G}\in\{0,1,2\}^{L} , where each coordinate counts the number of copies of a specified allele carried at each variant position. This representation is compact relative to the full genome, but L L still ranges from 10 5 10^{5} to 10 7 10^{7} correlated variants, and modern cohorts now include over 10 6 10^{6} participants, including UK Biobank ( > 500 ​ K >500{\rm K} ) [ 11 ] , FinnGen ( > 500 ​ K >500{\rm K} ) [ 30 ] , All of Us ( > 849 ​ K >849{\rm K} ) [ 7 ] , and the Million Veteran Program ( > 10 6 >10^{6} ) [ 22 ] . Synthetic genome generation thus requires modeling an ultra-high-dimensional discrete distribution in which disease-relevant signal is often highly sparse [ 58 , 8 ] . Recent progress in text, images, and proteins demonstrates that generative models for discrete data can scale when they exploit domain structure and learn compact representations of high-dimensional data [ 9 , 44 , 35 ] . SNP-level genomes present distinct challenges as they contain up to tens of millions of correlated discrete variants, and disease-relevant signal is distributed across many distant weak-effect loci. A practical generator must preserve genome-wide genetic data fidelity while capturing disease-relevant liability signals that can be used for conditional control in downstream analyses. Existing generative formulations are not fully aligned with this target. Base-level genomic foundation models [ 38 , 17 , 62 ] are typically trained on reference genome sequences and are thus focused on regulatory or functional prediction tasks, not modeling human genetic variation. Classical haplotype simulators and reference-panel methods reproduce local genetic structure but typically rely on fixed reference cohorts or phased haplotypes, where a haplotype refers to the allele sequence carried on one inherited chromosomal copy. Phasing infers the two inherited haplotype sequences from unphased genotype dosages and remains computationally intensive at biobank scale, often requiring approximate iterative algorithms [ 25 , 10 ] . Moreover, many methods target only small regions or GWAS-filtered variant sets, limiting genome-wide utility. Here, we introduce HELICS : H igh-fidelity g E neration via L atent I nterpolant C onditional S ynthesis, a scalable latent flow matching framework for genome-wide SNP-level generation. HELICS directly models unphased biobank-scale genetic data, compresses SNP sequences into continuous latent tokens, and learns a genome-wide latent flow model that supports conditional sampling. We rigorously evaluate HELICS against existing genotype-generation approaches using downstream genetics benchmarks that assess fidelity to real cohorts and diversity of generated samples. Finally, we show that HELICS supports conditional generation, moving synthetic genome generation toward controllable simulation of biologically meaningful variation. Our main contributions are: 1. Scalable phasing-free genome generation. We introduce a genome-wide framework that tokenizes SNP dosages and models multi-chromosome latent sequence with a transformer-based flow matching model trained directly on unphased biobank data. 2. High-fidelity synthetic genomes for downstream genetic analysis. HELICS generates synthetic cohorts that preserve key structure for downstream genetic analysis, including allele-frequency (AF) spectra, linkage disequilibrium (LD; local SNP correlation), ancestry geometry, and generated diversity. 3. Controllable generation of genetic-liability profiles. HELICS conditions on ancestry and genetic-liability summaries to generate genomes with targeted polygenic profiles while retaining genome-wide realism. Perturbation of the conditional genetic liability induces SNP-level dosage changes that align with external GWAS effects, providing an interpretable check on conditional control.

sections.heading: 2.1 Synthetic genotype generators
sections.text: Synthetic genotype generation has traditionally relied on haplotype simulators and reference-panel methods such as HAPGEN2 [ 50 ] , Sim1000G [ 19 ] , and HAPNEST [ 56 ] . Rather than learning a flexible distribution over genotype dosage data, these methods rely on phased reference panels. HAPGEN2 and HAPNEST generate genomes by recombining phased haplotypes in the observed reference panel, whereas Sim1000G estimates regional statistical moments and samples thresholded multivariate Gaussian variables. Learned genotype generators, including GAN- [ 60 ] and diffusion-based approaches [ 31 , 29 ] , provide more flexible modeling but are restricted to small genomic regions, single chromosomes, or small trait-associated SNP subsets. These restrictions limit their practical utility for biobank-scale synthetic data generation and can exclude fine-scale genotype structure such as weak polygenic signals outside predefined associated loci. Appendix E provides a detailed discussion of the assumptions and tradeoffs underlying each class of method. Conditional generation has been widely implemented in biomedical imaging [ 21 , 42 , 27 , 28 ] and “digital-twin” clinical modeling [ 49 , 51 ] , where generative models are used to simulate samples under specified attributes or counterfactual conditions. Yet this area remains underdeveloped for genome-wide genotype generation. Existing trait-conditioned genotype models typically require a predefined trait-relevant SNP set [ 31 ] , which limits their applicability to highly polygenic traits, where genetic risk is distributed across many variants of individually small effect, and to discovery settings, where the conditionally relevant variants are not known in advance. A critical open problem is to learn disease-relevant structures from genome-wide variation, rather than restricting generation to variants preselected by external association tests. Existing genotype generators do not address that setting which we target in this work, namely whole-genome controllable generation, learned directly from unphased biobank-scale dosage data.

sections.heading: 2.2 Base-level genomic sequence models
sections.text: A separate line of work has advanced base-level DNA modeling through long-context architectures, bidirectional objectives, and learned tokenization for nucleotide strings [ 20 , 62 , 17 , 38 ] . These models are mainly designed for regulatory, functional, and molecular prediction tasks over sequences in { A , C , G , T } \{A,C,G,T\} . For population and disease genetics, the relevant object is often different as individuals share most of the reference genome. Phenotypic or ancestry differences are instead commonly studied at sites of human genetic variation, especially SNPs, represented as allele dosages across individuals. Because genome-wide association studies, polygenic risk scoring, ancestry inference, and many biobank-scale analyses are formulated at the variant level, we focus on SNP-level generation rather than base-level DNA sequence generation.

sections.heading: 2.3 Latent generative modeling for high-dimensional data
sections.text: High-dimensional generative modeling often relies on learned latent representations. Latent diffusion and flow models encode observations into a lower-dimensional space and learn a latent space transport map which reduces computational cost [ 46 , 52 ] . Recent high-compression autoencoders further show that latent quality and structure can strongly affect downstream generative fidelity [ 15 , 16 ] . This strategy is especially useful for genome-scale SNP data, where direct discrete modeling would require operating over hundreds of thousands to millions of categorical coordinates. Autoregressive and discrete-diffusion models provide alternatives for discrete data [ 53 , 26 , 4 ] , but autoregressive models impose a unidirectional factorization that is not clearly justified for genotype data, and direct categorical denoising is difficult to scale to tens of millions of SNPs. We thus combine flexible genotype encoders with flow matching in a learned continuous latent space.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem setup
sections.text: We represent each individual genome as a collection of chromosome-indexed variant dosage sequences. For individual i i and chromosome c ∈ { 1 , … , 22 } c\in\{1,\ldots,22\} , HELICS takes as input 𝑮 c , i ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } L c \boldsymbol{G}_{c,i}\in\{0,1,2\}^{L_{c}} , where L c L_{c} is the number of retained variants on chromosome c c , and each entry denotes the dosage at a given SNP. Variants are ordered by genomic position; unlike other biological data modalities where features have no meaningful ordering (e.g. single-cell or proteomic data), genomic variants are not exchangeable since local dependence is induced by LD and shared haplotypic structure. HELICS directly models unphased genotype dosages across the genome, unlike many existing approaches, and avoids a computationally expensive preprocessing step at biobank scale. Leveraging the wealth of data available in modern large-scale biobanks, we train our generative models on UK Biobank (UKB) genotype data. Use of UKB data was approved under application 52008. After data preprocessing and quality control (see Appendix A.1 ), the data comprised 604,243 604{,}243 autosomal SNPs and 427,948 427{,}948 individuals across multiple ancestries, of which 10,000 10{,}000 individuals were held out as a validation set and the rest were used for training the HELICS multi-ancestry model. We also train a single-ancestry version of HELICS for which the training data comprised 251,465 251{,}465 unrelated self-reported White British individuals.

(a) A conditional USiT model architecture is used to learn a velocity field over concatenated chromosome latent tokens. (b) Synthetic genomes are generated by integrating over the learned velocity field, splitting generated tokens by chromosome and decoding with trained decoders. We parameterize v θ v_{\theta} with USiT, an SiT-style latent transformer adapted from DC-AE generative modeling [ 15 ] , combining UViT [ 6 ] with the SiT sampler [ 34 ] . USiT applies full self-attention over the concatenated multi-chromosome latent tokens with learned positional, chromosome, time, and condition embeddings, plus lightweight source-aware token adapters (Figure 2 a). Genome-wide experiments use a U-shaped variant with H H encoder-to-decoder skip connections to preserve token-level information during global processing (Figure B2 ); architectural details are in Appendix B.2 . At generation time, we sample 𝒁 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝑰 ) \boldsymbol{Z}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\boldsymbol{I}) and integrate the learned vector field with DPM-Solver++ [ 33 ] to obtain a generated latent 𝒁 ^ \widehat{\boldsymbol{Z}} . Chromosome-specific decoders then partition and map 𝒁 ^ \widehat{\boldsymbol{Z}} to make genotype calls (Figure 2 b). For multi-ancestry HELICS, we apply two additional post-training decoder refinement procedures; decoder-side refinement is a standard procedure in compressed latent models [ 14 , 61 , 13 ] . In the latent space, generated tokens undergo spectral projection onto token-specific subspaces explaining 99 % 99\% of training latent variance; this removes generated variation along low-variance token directions that are poorly supported by the training latent distribution. In the genotype space, genotype calls undergo a fixed low-rank PC alignment to the training genotypes. Importantly, spectral statistics are estimated from training latents, and PC alignment is fitted once using training genotypes and a fixed generated refinement sample. These refinement procedures are frozen and applied unchanged to every subsequent generation using no held-out evaluation data. These refinements form an essential final stage of the HELICS model-fitting procedure; the unrefined generator represents an intermediate state rather than an intended model endpoint. Reported multi-ancestry fidelity reflects the complete refined generator. Details and ablations are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 3.4 Controllable trait-guided generation
sections.text: We condition generation on target profiles 𝒄 i \boldsymbol{c}_{i} comprising ancestry coordinates and discretized genetic liabilities to a set of preselected traits. In training, we compute polygenic risk scores (PRS) for each trait k k and individual i i , PRS i ​ k = ∑ j ∈ 𝒮 k β j ​ k ​ G i ​ j , \mathrm{PRS}_{ik}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{k}}\beta_{jk}G_{ij}, where 𝒮 k \mathcal{S}_{k} denotes matched score variants, β j ​ k \beta_{jk} is the published effect size for variant j j , and G i ​ j G_{ij} is the effect-allele dosage. Trait selection, PRS sources, and preprocessing are detailed in Appendix D . We assign each PRS to a decile bin and use decile labels and ancestry coordinates given by the top 20 genetic principal components, as the conditioning profile. At generation time, specifying a target bin controls the desired genetic liability stratum. Conditioning is applied in both stages of the model. The autoencoder injects a learned embedding τ η ​ ( 𝒄 i ) \tau_{\eta}(\boldsymbol{c}_{i}) via FiLM-style modulation [ 41 ] , and the latent flow model learns v θ ​ ( 𝒁 t , t , 𝒄 i ) v_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{Z}_{t},t,\boldsymbol{c}_{i}) using DiT-style adaLN-Zero modulation and a concatenated condition token [ 40 ] . Main results use standard conditional sampling, equivalent to classifier-free guidance with scale 1.0 1.0 [ 24 ] ; guided sampling is evaluated in Appendix D.3 . In Section 4.4 , we assess control by conditioning on held-out validation profiles 𝒄 i \boldsymbol{c}_{i} and comparing generated genotypes to their observed counterparts.

sections.heading: 4.1 Evaluation setup
sections.text: We evaluate HELICS against the UKB [ 11 ] , the training source for HELICS; 1000 Genomes (1KG) [ 5 ] , the reference panel used by several haplotype-based baselines; and NHGRI Centers for Common Disease Genomics (CCDG) [ 45 ] , an external population-scale cohort ( N ≈ 140 ​ K N\approx 140\mathrm{K} ). We consider EUR-ancestry benchmarks here. HELICS generates genome-wide data, but since several prior methods are limited to the regional panel of [ 60 ] , benchmarks use harmonized common variants on chromosome 15 across UKB/1KG/CCDG after filtering to MAF > 1 % >1\% , yielding 18,784 18{,}784 SNPs; each method is evaluated on its available overlap with this harmonized SNP set. We compare HELICS and HELICS-EUR (a single-ancestry model trained only on EUR UKB samples) to haplotype simulators HAPNEST [ 56 ] , HAPGEN2 [ 50 ] , and Sim1000G [ 19 ] , and released learned generators based on GANs, restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) [ 60 ] , and hierarchical latent tree (HCLT) models [ 18 ] . Many existing generators are designed for restricted genomic panels or smaller reference cohorts and cannot readily leverage a full UKB training set. We hence evaluate these methods under their stated settings and emphasize that regional genotype generators constitute much of the existing literature. Scaling to both genome-wide variant panels and biobank-sized training cohorts is a central contribution of HELICS. Training-size and reference-panel sensitivity analyses and additional benchmarking details for all baseline methods are provided in Appendix F . Metrics quantify genetic data fidelity, privacy proxies, and generated diversity. Allele-frequency fidelity compares generated and reference MAFs, namely the frequencies of the less common alleles, using R 2 R^{2} and MAE. LD fidelity compares local SNP correlation structure using the length-normalized Frobenius norm of the difference between generated and reference LD matrices (smaller values indicate closer LD). Population structure is assessed by projection into reference genotype-PC space. Membership signal measures whether nearest-neighbor (NN) distance from real individuals to the generated cohort separates UKB training from held-out validation samples, reported as | AUC − 0.5 | |\mathrm{AUC}-0.5| , with values near zero indicating little train-validation separability; this is a proxy for privacy. Generated NN IBS similarity measures within-synthetic nearest-neighbor identity-by-state (IBS) similarity, where lower values suggest more diversity and reduced mode collapse. More detailed definitions of these metrics and additional benchmarks are included in Appendix F .

HELICS shows strong overall performance. The multi-ancestry model achieves the strongest overall MAF agreement, while HELICS-EUR achieves the lowest LD discrepancy and strong low-frequency MAF agreement, as expected under ancestry-matched training. Regional reference-based simulators such as Sim1000G and HAPGEN2 are included for completeness and remain competitive for low-frequency variants, but their unconditional regional sampling is substantially narrower in scope than HELICS’s joint genome-wide, trait-conditioned generation from biobank-scale data. Local learned generators have fewer overlapping SNPs and are generally outperformed here. HELICS combines strong genetic fidelity with genome-wide generation from unphased dosages and trait conditioning. Membership and diversity metrics show no evidence of substantial leakage or copying. HELICS models have membership deviations near reference baselines and comparable to the best-performing baselines, as well as NN IBS similarity close to the UKB control for HELICS-EUR. sections.heading: 4.3 Latent space captures human genetic structure
sections.text: We next characterize the learned latent space and find that its dominant geometry reflects genetic ancestry structure. Each individual is represented by a latent tensor 𝒁 i ∈ ℝ T × d \boldsymbol{Z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} . For visualization, we standardize each token-coordinate across individuals, compute normalized Frobenius distances between latent tensors, and apply UMAP [ 37 ] with the resulting distance matrix. Note that UMAP is used only as a qualitative visualization of this tokenized latent geometry. Figure 4: Genome-wide latents preserve human genetic structure. (a) UKB genotype PCs for 100,000 100{,}000 individuals colored by self-reported ancestry. (b) UMAP of held-out validation latents ( N = 5,000 N=5{,}000 ) using token-standardized Frobenius distances. (c) Real and generated latents overlap in the same embedding. (d) The embedding colored by genotype PCs shows preserved axes of genetic variation. Figure 4 shows that the learned latent space preserves major axes of human genetic variation. Held-out individuals organize by self-reported ancestry in the latent space, and genotype PCs vary continuously across this embedding. HELICS also shows strong coverage of the population variation on the UMAP coordinates, indicating that the model captures diverse ancestries in heterogeneous populations like the UKB. Chromosome-specific visualizations and coverage metrics in Appendix G show similar real/generated correspondence. We quantify latent alignment within self-reported ancestry groups using sliced W 2 W_{2} with 512 random projections and RBF MMD 2 in the top 250 latent-PC space (Table G5 ). Alignment is strongest for the majority White group and weaker for underrepresented groups, consistent with their smaller training sample sizes. Ancestry-stratified genotype evaluation likewise shows weaker fidelity in underrepresented groups (Table G4 ).

sections.heading: 4.4 Genetic liability condition perturbations reveal interpretable SNP-level changes
sections.text: Figure 5: Conditional PRS control schematic. HELICS generates 𝑮 ~ i \widetilde{\boldsymbol{G}}_{i} conditional on a validation profile 𝒄 i \boldsymbol{c}_{i} . We next ask whether HELICS captures trait-relevant SNP-level genetic structure beyond ancestry and aggregate PRS control. To do so, we first assess conditional control using the procedure illustrated in Figure 5 . We focus on high-density lipoprotein (HDL) liability; HDL is a clinically relevant blood-lipid trait involved in cardiovascular risk, making it a useful test case for interpretable genetic-liability control. For each held-out validation individual i i , we use HELICS to generate 𝑮 ~ i \widetilde{\boldsymbol{G}}_{i} from that individual’s conditioning profile 𝒄 i \boldsymbol{c}_{i} , including ancestry PCs and trait PRS deciles. We then compute HDL PRS from 𝑮 ~ i \widetilde{\boldsymbol{G}}_{i} and compare it to the HDL PRS of the corresponding observed genotype 𝑮 i \boldsymbol{G}_{i} . The generated and observed HDL PRSs are highly correlated ( r = 0.662 r=0.662 ), indicating effective conditional control as the conditional signal for HDL liability is preserved in the generated genomes. Further, rescoring with a separate HDL score not used for conditioning shows that positive generated-observed correlation persists after filtering variants in strong LD with the HDL conditioning-score variants (Appendix D.2 ). sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced HELICS, a scalable latent flow matching framework for SNP-level genome generation trained directly on unphased biobank data. By combining chromosome-specific encoding with a multi-chromosome latent flow, HELICS enables high-fidelity genome-wide synthesis at a scale beyond many existing genotype generators, preserving AF spectra, LD, ancestry structure, and sample diversity. Trait-guided experiments further show that perturbing genetic-liability profiles induces dosage shifts aligned with published association effects, despite the high dimensionality and polygenicity of the target traits. Several directions remain to extend HELICS. Augmenting association studies of underrepresented cohorts or difficult-to-measure traits is an important next step, but requires robust statistical frameworks that preserve inferential validity and control inflation under synthetic data augmentation [ 2 ] . HELICS is currently limited to common variants; future work should also extend HELICS to denser whole-genome panels including rare variants. Fidelity is weaker for low-frequency variants, and underrepresented ancestry groups show poorer latent alignment and PRS recovery. Transfer-learning strategies can be incorporated for underrepresented ancestries and imbalanced disease cohorts. Our perturbation analyses demonstrate that HELICS learns trait-associated patterns of genotype variation from genome-wide data and coarse liability summaries. This motivates further investigations into how HELICS represents shared genetic variation across traits and among distant loci. Further, conditioning on measured phenotypes and clinical covariates could support discovery of new genetic associations. These extensions can also enable sharing synthetic individual-level data for richer cross-cohort meta-analyses beyond marginal association summaries, provided sufficient fidelity, privacy, and inferential calibration can be achieved. Overall, conditional synthetic genome generation offers both a demanding use case for scalable generative modeling of structured discrete data and a promising tool for benchmarking, privacy-aware access, and controlled genetic simulation.

sections.heading: Organization of the Appendix
sections.text: The appendix is organized as follows. We first describe data construction in Appendix A , including UK Biobank preprocessing, external reference cohorts, ancestry assignment, and variant harmonization. In Appendix B , we describe the architectural and training details for HELICS, from chromosome-specific autoencoders to the latent flow matching model. Appendix C describes the post-training refinement procedure used for multi-ancestry generation and ablates its components. Appendix D defines the conditioning variables used for controlled generation and examines classifier-free guidance. We then review existing synthetic genome generators in Appendix E and describe the benchmark construction, baseline generation procedures, and evaluation metrics in Appendix F . Finally, Appendix G reports additional fidelity and relatedness results.

sections.heading: A.1 UK Biobank data processing
sections.text: We used UK Biobank autosomal SNP genotype data derived from array-based genotyping and imputation. Starting from 488,377 individuals from the filtered data release, we retained variants on chromosomes 1-22 and applied sample and variant quality control using PLINK [ 12 ] : individual missingness ---mind 0.02 , variant missingness ---geno 0.20 , minor allele frequency ---maf 0.01 , and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium ---hwe 1e-12 . After quality control, the dataset comprised 427,948 individuals and 604,243 variants, with an overall genotyping rate of 0.9911. We reserved 10,000 individuals for held-out testing and benchmarking. From the remaining samples, we used 251,465 unrelated British White individuals to train HELICS-EUR. An additional 42,669 British White individuals were retained for validation analyses, including hyperparameter tuning, phenotype-association evaluations, and exploratory analyses. We provide detailed methodological descriptions and have released implementation code at https://github.com/ahmadazim/HELICS . Due to the sensitivity of UKB genomic data release regulations, the training data and trained models are not publicly available. A public-data example is included; the demo downloads 1KG-EUR chr22, trains HELICS end to end, generates synthetic genotypes, and evaluates generated data fidelity.

sections.heading: A.2 External reference cohorts: 1000 Genomes and CCDG
sections.text: We used two external multi-ancestry reference cohorts for benchmarking and ancestry harmonization: the 1000 Genomes Project (1KG) [ 5 ] and the NHGRI Centers for Common Disease Genomics (CCDG) [ 45 ] . The 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 release comprises 2,504 individuals from 26 populations and was carefully designed as a broad reference panel for human genetic variation across several continental ancestry groups [ 5 ] . We include the 1KG cohort here since many of the baseline methods we benchmarked either use 1KG as their reference panel or require phased reference haplotypes. Since the 1KG Phase 3 haplotypes are publicly available in phased form, methods requiring phased input were run directly from the provided phased release without additional phasing. We include the CCDG cohort as an external validation set to assess generalization beyond the training source or reference panel of all methods. CCDG is a large-scale NHGRI genome-sequencing effort designed to identify variants contributing to common disease phenotypes, with approximately 140 ​ K 140\rm{K} whole genomes sequenced [ 45 ] . Although CCDG samples were collected through disease-focused studies largely based in the United States, we did not rely on study labels or self-reported ancestry; genetic ancestry was inferred by projection into a 1KG-defined genetic-PC reference space. Briefly, we fit genotype PCs on 1KG reference samples with known superpopulation labels, projected each target sample into this PC space, and assigned ancestry by nearest-neighbor matching to the projected 1KG samples based on the top 20 PCs. This retained the 43,828 CCDG samples assigned closest to EUR ancestry for the EUR benchmark. We used the 1KG cohort as the ancestry reference since it is a highly curated diverse reference panel with standardized population labels, as opposed to self-reported ancestry. Accordingly, 1KG was used to define the reference ancestry space for assigning EUR subsets, as described above, across generated samples, baseline methods, UKB, and CCDG.

sections.heading: A.3 Variant harmonization
sections.text: Genotype data and baseline outputs were harmonized to a common chromosome and allele representation before benchmarking. We lifted all datasets to a common genome build (GRCh37) using bcftools liftover [ 23 ] . After liftover, we retained autosomal biallelic common SNPs present across the reference datasets and matched variants by target-build position and unordered allele pair. The UKB data were used to define the canonical coordinate system and A1/A2 allele coding. For each reference or generated dataset, we applied A1/A2 recoding, allele swaps, and strand flips as needed to match the UKB convention; ambiguously matched variants were excluded. We then subset each benchmarked method to its overlap with this harmonized reference set. For chromosome 15, for example, this procedure produced a final benchmark reference panel of 18,784 18{,}784 harmonized variants.

sections.heading: B.1 Chromosome-specific autoencoders
sections.text: HELICS trains one convolutional autoencoder per chromosome to tokenize the input genome-wide data. For chromosome c c , the encoder maps an unphased dosage sequence 𝑮 c ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } L c \boldsymbol{G}_{c}\in\{0,1,2\}^{L_{c}} to a sequence of continuous latent tokens 𝒁 c ∈ ℝ T c × d , \boldsymbol{Z}_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{c}\times d}, where L c L_{c} is the number of retained SNPs on chromosome c c , T c T_{c} is the chromosome-specific latent token count, and d = 256 d=256 is the shared latent token dimension. The decoder then maps 𝒁 c \boldsymbol{Z}_{c} back to per-SNP genotype logits over the three dosage classes { 0 , 1 , 2 } \{0,1,2\} . All chromosome-specific latents are concatenated before training the genome-wide latent flow model.

The encoder then applies N c down N_{c}^{\mathrm{down}} residual downsampling blocks. sections.heading: B.1.5 Regularization ablations
sections.text: We ablate the auxiliary loss terms to assess whether they improve reconstruction fidelity and the suitability of the latent space for downstream flow matching. We do this by comparing validation performance at the final epoch before λ reg > 0 \lambda_{\rm reg}>0 to the final epoch of autoencoder training (Figure B1 ). We see regularization does not degrade reconstruction accuracy; validation MSE is lower at the final regularized epoch for most chromosomes. The largest effect is on the latent TV penalty, which drops sharply after regularization, suggesting that the token latents become substantially smoother. Robustness and stability penalties also decrease, indicating that the learned latent representation becomes less sensitive to latent and input-embedding perturbations, which we posit provides a better-conditioned representation for downstream flow matching. Figure B1: Regularization ablation for chromosome-specific autoencoders. For each chromosome, we compare validation metrics at the last epoch before λ reg > 0 \lambda_{\rm reg}>0 , against the final epoch after regularization. Regularization consistently reduces latent total variation, robustness loss, and stability loss, while continuing to improve validation reconstruction MSE.

sections.heading: Appendix C Post-training refinement
sections.text: For the multi-ancestry HELICS model, we apply a post-training refinement procedure before final benchmarking, which includes token-wise spectral projection before decoding and genotype-space PC alignment followed by deterministic rounding after decoding. HELICS-EUR does not use these refinements. Spectral statistics are estimated from training latents. Genotype standardization, PCA bases, and alignment parameters are estimated once using training genotypes and a fixed generated calibration sample, then frozen. No CCDG or held-out evaluation-cohort information is used to fit these transformations. This closed-form decoder-side refinement is motivated by refinement strategies in compressed latent generative models [ 15 , 61 , 13 ] . For example, DC-AE architectures demonstrated that high-compression autoencoders benefit from including refinement steps to tune middle layers (adapt the latent space) and decoder head layers (improve local reconstruction without changing the full latent representation) [ 15 ] . We apply the same principle here using a token-wise latent refinement before decoding and a genotype-space PC alignment after decoding, instead of additional training.

sections.heading: Effect of token-wise spectral truncation.
sections.text: Figure C4 ablates the latent spectral correction. Without spectral truncation, generated samples collapse in genotype-PC space and fail to separate ancestry groups, even after decoding. Applying token-wise spectral thresholding before decoding restores the dominant ancestry geometry; namely, generated samples show the expected genetic ancestry structure and self-reported ancestry groups separate. This indicates that low-variance token directions in the generated latent distribution can decode into unstable population-structure artifacts. Removing these unsupported directions before decoding is therefore necessary for reliable multi-ancestry generation. Together, these ablations demonstrate that post-training refinement is a necessary component for multi-ancestry HELICS. Spectral truncation stabilizes generated latents before decoding, while genotype-space PC alignment corrects broad low-rank population-structure discrepancies in decoded genotypes. However, while the refinement improves PC alignment and recovers LD structure and MAF agreement, the final discretization step reduces low-frequency MAF agreement due to the discretization procedure.

sections.heading: Appendix E Existing synthetic genome generators
sections.text: We survey two broad classes of synthetic genotype generators: reference-panel simulators that rely on observed input haplotypes, and learned generators trained on fixed SNP panels. HAPGEN2 [ 50 ] is a classical haplotype-based simulator that generates synthetic genomes by simulating recombination or resampling haplotypic structure from the input reference panel. It was designed for simulating case-control datasets at SNP markers in particular, including settings with multiple disease SNPs on a chromosome. Sim1000G [ 19 ] estimates regional allele frequency and a dense covariance matrix and generates genotypes by thresholding multivariate Gaussian samples; this provides strong regional frequency fidelity observed in Table 1 . Dense covariance storage scales as O ⁡ ( L 2 ) O(L^{2}) and factorization as O ⁡ ( L 3 ) O(L^{3}) . A 604,243 × 604,243 604{,}243\times 604{,}243 double-precision covariance matrix alone requires approximately 2.9 2.9 TB, before factorization and other arrays. While inflexible and typically not scalable, these approaches are strong baselines for local haplotype realism as they preserve local correlation structure present in the reference panel. These approaches are best interpreted as reference-panel simulators as opposed to flexible genome-wide generative models. They preserve AF and local LD when the reference panel is well matched but are not suited for learning new genotype distributions from biobank-scale cohorts or for conditioning on genetic-liability profiles. HAPNEST [ 56 ] is a more recent reference-based simulator. Developed to generate large synthetic genotype and phenotype cohorts, it improves the scalability of haplotype-based simulation and was designed to preserve data fidelity while reducing close genetic relatedness to the reference panel. Nevertheless, HAPNEST remains tied to phased reference haplotype structure, so while it is a strong large-scale baseline, its reliance on phased genotypes and reference-panel based haplotype structure are serious limitations. Recent work [ 60 ] introduced deep generative models for artificial human genomes using generative adversarial networks (GANs) and restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs). These models were trained on phased haplotypes and evaluated on a small 10,000 10{,}000 -SNP chromosome 15 panel. While limited in terms of genomic scale, this work demonstrated that neural generators can in fact reproduce important properties of real genomic data, including AFs, LD, pairwise haplotype distances, and population structure. Nevertheless, dense neural generators trained directly on SNP haplotypes become difficult to scale as the number of variants grows. Later work used convolutional WGAN and conditional RBM models for larger genomic segments, including chromosome 1-scale panels [ 59 ] , but this line of work has yet to model genome-wide unphased dosage data. Hidden Chow-Liu tree (HCLT) models [ 18 ] provide a tractable probabilistic alternative to neural generators. HCLTs introduce latent variables and learn tree-structured dependencies among genomic variables, often represented as probabilistic circuits to enable efficient likelihood evaluation and sampling. HCLTs provide more explicit probabilistic structure and tractable inference than GANs for example, and their hidden variables increase expressivity over simple tree models to capture longer-range dependencies. In practice, however, the available HCLT-based synthetic genome benchmarks are also tied to restricted SNP panels and do not directly address genome-wide conditional generation from unphased genomes. Conditional control remains a key gap in synthetic genotype generation. Reference-panel simulators generate phenotypes after genotype simulation by specifying effect sizes, environmental noise, or covariate effects (namely, the objects we are typically interested in learning), and HAPNEST supports large-scale synthetic genotype–phenotype datasets for PRS benchmarking [ 56 ] . However, this is not the same as learning a conditional genotype distribution as the genotype is still generated from phased reference haplotype structure, and phenotypes are simply assigned downstream from the generative model. Direct control over genome-wide genotype generation under a target disease-liability is what HELICS offers to address the conditional genome generation gap. Recent diffusion-based genotype generators move toward this goal but make restrictive design choices. SNPgen [ 31 ] proposes a phenotype-supervised latent diffusion framework conditioned on binary disease labels, but first precedes generation with GWAS-guided variant selection and models only 1,024 1{,}024 – 2,048 2{,}048 trait-associated SNPs with a latent diffusion model. This limits applicability to highly polygenic traits, cross-trait analyses, and discovery settings where the relevant loci are not known in advance. Kenneweg et al. [ 29 ] also introduce a diffusion model for synthetic human genotypes, but achieve scalability by assigning SNPs to gene regions and using PCA within those regions, which may discard fine-scale nonlinear LD, weak polygenic effects outside selected loci, and long-range cross-chromosomal structure. Their trained models and generated cohorts needed for matched harmonized benchmarking are not released.

sections.heading: F.1 Baseline acquisition and generation
sections.text: We evaluated baselines using released synthetic data when available and otherwise generated samples from the published reproducible simulation procedures. For the GAN- and RBM-based methods [ 60 ] , released synthetic haplotypes were available on the chromosome 15 panel. Ancestry was inferred by matching synthetic haplotypes to 1KG reference haplotypes; EUR-assigned haplotypes were retained, and haplotypes were paired within ancestry to construct diploid dosage matrices. We applied the same procedure to the HCLT-based samples [ 18 ] , which were generated on the same reference panel. For HAPNEST [ 56 ] , we used the released synthetic dosage data directly and retained EUR-assigned samples after ancestry matching to 1KG. For HAPGEN2 [ 50 ] and Sim1000G [ 19 ] , we simulated synthetic individuals based on phased 1KG EUR haplotypes. Since Sim1000G is computationally expensive at larger variant counts, we simulated only a 10,000 10{,}000 -variant subset of chromosome 15. For every method, output variants were harmonized using the same build, allele, and strand-matching procedure described in Appendix A.3 .

sections.heading: F.3 Genetic data fidelity metrics
sections.text: To assess generated data fidelity, we evaluate several properties of the synthetic genomes which are motivated by downstream utility, such as marginal variation, local correlation, ancestry structure, memorization risk, and within-synthetic diversity. The following metrics are assessed in Table 1 : • Allele-frequency agreement. For each harmonized variant j j , we compute the minor allele frequency (MAF) in the generated cohort and in the reference cohort and report the R 2 R^{2} between generated and reference MAFs, the mean absolute error (MAE) MAE MAF = 1 m ​ ∑ j = 1 m | f ^ j gen − f ^ j ref | , \mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{MAF}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\widehat{f}^{\mathrm{gen}}_{j}-\widehat{f}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{j}\right|, and a low-frequency R 2 R^{2} restricted to variants with 0.01 < MAF < 0.05 0.01<\mathrm{MAF}<0.05 in the reference cohort. • LD fidelity. We measure correspondence between the generated and real genomes’ local SNP correlation structure. For each LD block or fixed genomic window b b , let 𝑹 b ref \boldsymbol{R}_{b}^{\mathrm{ref}} and 𝑹 b gen \boldsymbol{R}_{b}^{\mathrm{gen}} denote the reference and generated dosage correlation matrices over the variants in that block. We summarize LD distortion using a length-normalized Frobenius discrepancy, d LD ​ ( b ) = ‖ 𝑹 b gen − 𝑹 b ref ‖ F | b | , d_{\mathrm{LD}}(b)=\frac{\left\|\boldsymbol{R}_{b}^{\mathrm{gen}}-\boldsymbol{R}_{b}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right\|_{F}}{|b|}, and report the average across inferred LD blocks. Smaller values indicate closer preservation of local LD. LD blocks were inferred using PLINK with ---blocks no-pheno-req no-small-max-span , ---blocks-inform-frac 0.9 , ---blocks-max-kb 100000 , ---blocks-min-maf 0.01 , ---blocks-recomb-highci 0.6 , ---blocks-strong-highci 0.8301 , and ---blocks-strong-lowci 0.5001 . Blocks with insufficient variant overlap after harmonization ( < 20 <20 SNPs) are excluded. • Population structure. We assess whether generated samples occupy the same ancestry geometry as real samples. We fit genotype PCs on a reference cohort, standardizing variants using the reference mean and variance, and project generated samples into this fixed PC basis. Agreement is evaluated qualitatively by comparing the generated and reference distributions in PC space. • Membership signal. We use nearest-neighbor IBS similarity to the generated cohort as an empirical memorization proxy. For each real individual i i , either from the training set or a held-out validation set, we compute its maximum IBS similarity to any generated individual. We define this distance as pairwise global identity-by-state (IBS) similarity. Between individuals x x and y y as S ⁡ ( x , y ) = 1 − ∑ m ∈ ℳ x ​ y | G x ​ m − G y ​ m | 2 ​ | ℳ x ​ y | , S(x,y)=1-\frac{\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{xy}}|G_{xm}-G_{ym}|}{2|\mathcal{M}_{xy}|}, where ℳ x ​ y \mathcal{M}_{xy} is the set of variants nonmissing in both individuals. For each query individual x x , its nearest-neighbor similarity to a reference cohort ℛ \mathcal{R} is S NN ​ ( x , ℛ ) = max y ∈ ℛ ⁡ S ⁡ ( x , y ) . S_{\mathrm{NN}}(x,\mathcal{R})=\max_{y\in\mathcal{R}}S(x,y). Here, ℛ \mathcal{R} is the generated cohort and the query individuals are either training individuals or held-out validation individuals. We then test whether S NN ​ ( x , ℛ ) S_{\mathrm{NN}}(x,\mathcal{R}) distinguishes training from validation samples using ROC AUC, reporting | AUC − 0.5 | |\mathrm{AUC}-0.5| , where values near zero indicate that training and validation individuals are similarly close to the generated cohort, while larger values indicate stronger train-validation separability and possible memorization signal. This is not a formal privacy guarantee, but provides a matched empirical check for overfitting. • Generated nearest-neighbor IBS similarity. We measure within-synthetic diversity using nearest-neighbor IBS similarity among generated samples. For each generated individual, we compute its maximum IBS similarity to another generated individual and summarize the distribution. From the definitions above, ℛ \mathcal{R} here is the generated cohort itself and the self-match is excluded, so high S NN S_{\mathrm{NN}} indicates near-duplicate generated samples or mode collapse. Lower values indicate greater generated diversity. In addition to the nearest-neighbor IBS metrics above, we infer kinship using KING. While IBS nearest-neighbor similarity measures overall genotype similarity by allele sharing across matched variants, KING estimates kinship coefficients which are intended to reflect identity-by-descent-like relatedness categories; this provides an interpretable degree-of-relatedness summary. We apply KING in three settings. We first compare synthetic samples to the corresponding training reference panel to assess train proximity. For HELICS, the training reference is UKB, while for Sim1000G, HAPGEN2, and HAPNEST, the training reference is the 1KG cohort. We then compare held-out validation samples to the same training reference, providing a matched baseline for relatedness under each method’s harmonized variant set. We also estimate within-synthetic kinship to assess generated diversity; excess close relatedness among generated samples indicates duplication or mode collapse. Note that these results should be interpreted relatively rather than as calibrated genome-wide relatedness estimates. We therefore exclude small regional generators with substantially fewer variants, where kinship inference is less reliable and often inflated. On this relative chromosome 15 benchmark, HELICS produces no MZ-twin, first-degree, or second-degree synthetic-to-training relationships, and its third-degree synthetic-to-training count is below the matched validation-to-training baseline. Within the generated cohort, HELICS also shows no close within-synthetic relationships and fewer third-degree pairs than Sim1000G or HAPGEN2, supporting the IBS-based diversity analysis (Table G1 ).

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and introduction state the paper’s contributions as a scalable latent generative model for unphased genome-wide SNP dosage data, with evaluations of fidelity, diversity, privacy-proxy behavior, ancestry structure, and conditional generation. These claims are supported by the main experiments and are scoped to the evaluated UKB, 1KG, CCDG, and baseline benchmark settings. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper discusses several limitations such as the use of empirical memorization proxies rather than formal privacy guarantees, the need for statistically robust frameworks to leverage synthetic data for downstream inference and discovery, and the restriction to common variants. These limitations are discussed throughout in the main text. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not make formal theoretical claims or present theorems requiring proof. Mathematical expressions are used to define the model, training objectives, and evaluation metrics, with implementation details provided in the methods and appendix. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper and appendix specify the data preprocessing, variant harmonization, model architecture, training objectives, hyperparameters, generation procedure, calibration procedure, baselines, and evaluation metrics needed to reproduce the experimental pipeline. Exact reproduction of UKB-trained models requires authorized access to the genotype data, but the methodological details needed to replicate the experiments under this data access are provided in Appendix A , Appendix B , Appendix D , and Appendix F . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [No] Justification: Due to access restrictions and participant privacy, individual-level UK Biobank genotypes and derived individual-level genomic data cannot be publicly redistributed. We provide detailed methodological and experimental specifications in the paper and appendix, and release code implementing the HELICS architecture and training pipeline (See Appendix A ); the released code contains the model implementation and enables reproduction by researchers with access to the same datasets. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.36361v1 [q-bio.GN] 26 Oct 2026 HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching Ahmad Abdel-Azim Affiliation: Department of Biostatistics Affiliation: Harvard University Affiliation: Boston, MA 02135 Email: ahmad_abdelazim@g.harvard.edu Xihong Lin Affiliation: Department of Statistics, Biostatistics Affiliation: Harvard University Affiliation: Boston, MA 02135 Email: xlin@hsph.harvard.edu Abstract Individual-level genotype data underpin genetic discovery, disease-risk modeling, and therapeutic development, yet many critical settings remain data-limited, including underrepresented ancestries, rare or imbalanced disease cohorts, and restricted-access biobanks. Conditional synthetic genome generation would support privacy-aware benchmarking, simulation, and data augmentation, but requires learning an ultra-high-dimensional discrete distribution over hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of correlated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), or sites of DNA variation. We introduce HELICS : H igh-fidelity g E neration via L atent I nterpolant C onditional S ynthesis, a phasing-free latent flow matching framework for genome-wide SNP-level generation from biobank-scale genotype data. HELICS tokenizes chromosomes with convolutional autoencoders, reducing > > 600 ​ K 600{\rm K} SNPs to 4,096 4{,}096 continuous latent tokens, and trains a transformer parameterized conditional flow matching model over the concatenated multi-chromosome latent representation. Trained on over 417 ​ K 417\rm K genomes in the UK Biobank, HELICS generates genome-wide common-variant synthetic cohorts without haplotype phasing and achieves stronger fidelity to held-out real genotypes than existing haplotype- and genotype-based simulators, including high allele-frequency agreement in external evaluation ( R 2 = 0.992 R^{2}=0.992 ) and superior preservation of local and long-range SNP correlation structure. Conditioning on ancestry and genetic liability summaries enables targeted generation across genetic risk profiles; in perturbation analyses, by increasing the conditioned disease trait liability, HELICS induces SNP-level dosage changes in generated genomes that are highly correlated with published association weights. HELICS provides a scalable generative modeling framework for SNP-level genome data and a path toward conditional synthetic cohorts for data-limited genetic studies. 1 Introduction Modern genetic studies increasingly depend on large cohorts of individual-level genotype data, motivating major investments in biobanks for genome-wide association studies (GWAS), polygenic risk modeling, and therapeutic target discovery. However, collecting genotype data at the scale needed to answer crucial scientific questions remains slow and costly. Existing cohorts are highly imbalanced across ancestries, biasing discovery toward well-represented populations; many diseases are rare and have small sample sizes; and individual-level data are sensitive, identifiable, and access-controlled. These common data-scarce settings motivate synthetic genome generation not only as a privacy mechanism, but importantly, as a way to construct realistic, controllable genotypes to support method development, fairer and more powerful analyses of underrepresented ancestries, and even discovery of genetic mechanisms relevant to disease and therapeutic development. Rather than modeling the four-letter DNA sequence directly, population-scale genetic analyses typically focus on specific sites of genomic variation known as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). SNPs are the primary coordinates used to link genetic differences across individuals to disease risk, complex traits, and population history [ 1 , 55 , 3 , 39 ] . Many genetic analyses focus on common variants (observed in >1% of the population) as they are well-powered for association testing and capture substantial polygenic variation. SNPs are represented as dosage vectors 𝑮 ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } L \boldsymbol{G}\in\{0,1,2\}^{L} , where each coordinate counts the number of copies of a specified allele carried at each variant position. This representation is compact relative to the full genome, but L L still ranges from 10 5 10^{5} to 10 7 10^{7} correlated variants, and modern cohorts now include over 10 6 10^{6} participants, including UK Biobank ( > 500 ​ K >500{\rm K} ) [ 11 ] , FinnGen ( > 500 ​ K >500{\rm K} ) [ 30 ] , All of Us ( > 849 ​ K >849{\rm K} ) [ 7 ] , and the Million Veteran Program ( > 10 6 >10^{6} ) [ 22 ] . Synthetic genome generation thus requires modeling an ultra-high-dimensional discrete distribution in which disease-relevant signal is often highly sparse [ 58 , 8 ] . Recent progress in text, images, and proteins demonstrates that generative models for discrete data can scale when they exploit domain structure and learn compact representations of high-dimensional data [ 9 , 44 , 35 ] . SNP-level genomes present distinct challenges as they contain up to tens of millions of correlated discrete variants, and disease-relevant signal is distributed across many distant weak-effect loci. A practical generator must preserve genome-wide genetic data fidelity while capturing disease-relevant liability signals that can be used for conditional control in downstream analyses. Existing generative formulations are not fully aligned with this target. Base-level genomic foundation models [ 38 , 17 , 62 ] are typically trained on reference genome sequences and are thus focused on regulatory or functional prediction tasks, not modeling human genetic variation. Classical haplotype simulators and reference-panel methods reproduce local genetic structure but typically rely on fixed reference cohorts or phased haplotypes, where a haplotype refers to the allele sequence carried on one inherited chromosomal copy. Phasing infers the two inherited haplotype sequences from unphased genotype dosages and remains computationally intensive at biobank scale, often requiring approximate iterative algorithms [ 25 , 10 ] . Moreover, many methods target only small regions or GWAS-filtered variant sets, limiting genome-wide utility. Here, we introduce HELICS : H igh-fidelity g E neration via L atent I nterpolant C onditional S ynthesis, a scalable latent flow matching framework for genome-wide SNP-level generation. HELICS directly models unphased biobank-scale genetic data, compresses SNP sequences into continuous latent tokens, and learns a genome-wide latent flow model that supports conditional sampling. We rigorously evaluate HELICS against existing genotype-generation approaches using downstream genetics benchmarks that assess fidelity to real cohorts and diversity of generated samples. Finally, we show that HELICS supports conditional generation, moving synthetic genome generation toward controllable simulation of biologically meaningful variation. Our main contributions are: 1. Scalable phasing-free genome generation. We introduce a genome-wide framework that tokenizes SNP dosages and models multi-chromosome latent sequence with a transformer-based flow matching model trained directly on unphased biobank data. 2. High-fidelity synthetic genomes for downstream genetic analysis. HELICS generates synthetic cohorts that preserve key structure for downstream genetic analysis, including allele-frequency (AF) spectra, linkage disequilibrium (LD; local SNP correlation), ancestry geometry, and generated diversity. 3. Controllable generation of genetic-liability profiles. HELICS conditions on ancestry and genetic-liability summaries to generate genomes with targeted polygenic profiles while retaining genome-wide realism. Perturbation of the conditional genetic liability induces SNP-level dosage changes that align with external GWAS effects, providing an interpretable check on conditional control. 2 Related Work 2.1 Synthetic genotype generators Synthetic genotype generation has traditionally relied on haplotype simulators and reference-panel methods such as HAPGEN2 [ 50 ] , Sim1000G [ 19 ] , and HAPNEST [ 56 ] . Rather than learning a flexible distribution over genotype dosage data, these methods rely on phased reference panels. HAPGEN2 and HAPNEST generate genomes by recombining phased haplotypes in the observed reference panel, whereas Sim1000G estimates regional statistical moments and samples thresholded multivariate Gaussian variables. Learned genotype generators, including GAN- [ 60 ] and diffusion-based approaches [ 31 , 29 ] , provide more flexible modeling but are restricted to small genomic regions, single chromosomes, or small trait-associated SNP subsets. These restrictions limit their practical utility for biobank-scale synthetic data generation and can exclude fine-scale genotype structure such as weak polygenic signals outside predefined associated loci. Appendix E provides a detailed discussion of the assumptions and tradeoffs underlying each class of method. Conditional generation has been widely implemented in biomedical imaging [ 21 , 42 , 27 , 28 ] and “digital-twin” clinical modeling [ 49 , 51 ] , where generative models are used to simulate samples under specified attributes or counterfactual conditions. Yet this area remains underdeveloped for genome-wide genotype generation. Existing trait-conditioned genotype models typically require a predefined trait-relevant SNP set [ 31 ] , which limits their applicability to highly polygenic traits, where genetic risk is distributed across many variants of individually small effect, and to discovery settings, where the conditionally relevant variants are not known in advance. A critical open problem is to learn disease-relevant structures from genome-wide variation, rather than restricting generation to variants preselected by external association tests. Existing genotype generators do not address that setting which we target in this work, namely whole-genome controllable generation, learned directly from unphased biobank-scale dosage data. 2.2 Base-level genomic sequence models A separate line of work has advanced base-level DNA modeling through long-context architectures, bidirectional objectives, and learned tokenization for nucleotide strings [ 20 , 62 , 17 , 38 ] . These models are mainly designed for regulatory, functional, and molecular prediction tasks over sequences in { A , C , G , T } \{A,C,G,T\} . For population and disease genetics, the relevant object is often different as individuals share most of the reference genome. Phenotypic or ancestry differences are instead commonly studied at sites of human genetic variation, especially SNPs, represented as allele dosages across individuals. Because genome-wide association studies, polygenic risk scoring, ancestry inference, and many biobank-scale analyses are formulated at the variant level, we focus on SNP-level generation rather than base-level DNA sequence generation. 2.3 Latent generative modeling for high-dimensional data High-dimensional generative modeling often relies on learned latent representations. Latent diffusion and flow models encode observations into a lower-dimensional space and learn a latent space transport map which reduces computational cost [ 46 , 52 ] . Recent high-compression autoencoders further show that latent quality and structure can strongly affect downstream generative fidelity [ 15 , 16 ] . This strategy is especially useful for genome-scale SNP data, where direct discrete modeling would require operating over hundreds of thousands to millions of categorical coordinates. Autoregressive and discrete-diffusion models provide alternatives for discrete data [ 53 , 26 , 4 ] , but autoregressive models impose a unidirectional factorization that is not clearly justified for genotype data, and direct categorical denoising is difficult to scale to tens of millions of SNPs. We thus combine flexible genotype encoders with flow matching in a learned continuous latent space. 3 Method 3.1 Problem setup We represent each individual genome as a collection of chromosome-indexed variant dosage sequences. For individual i i and chromosome c ∈ { 1 , … , 22 } c\in\{1,\ldots,22\} , HELICS takes as input 𝑮 c , i ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } L c \boldsymbol{G}_{c,i}\in\{0,1,2\}^{L_{c}} , where L c L_{c} is the number of retained variants on chromosome c c , and each entry denotes the dosage at a given SNP. Variants are ordered by genomic position; unlike other biological data modalities where features have no meaningful ordering (e.g. single-cell or proteomic data), genomic variants are not exchangeable since local dependence is induced by LD and shared haplotypic structure. HELICS directly models unphased genotype dosages across the genome, unlike many existing approaches, and avoids a computationally expensive preprocessing step at biobank scale. Leveraging the wealth of data available in modern large-scale biobanks, we train our generative models on UK Biobank (UKB) genotype data. Use of UKB data was approved under application 52008. After data preprocessing and quality control (see Appendix A.1 ), the data comprised 604,243 604{,}243 autosomal SNPs and 427,948 427{,}948 individuals across multiple ancestries, of which 10,000 10{,}000 individuals were held out as a validation set and the rest were used for training the HELICS multi-ancestry model. We also train a single-ancestry version of HELICS for which the training data comprised 251,465 251{,}465 unrelated self-reported White British individuals. 3.2 Latent token representation Figure 1: Chromosome-specific conditional autoencoder architecture. Metrics quantify genetic data fidelity, privacy proxies, and generated diversity. Allele-frequency fidelity compares generated and reference MAFs, namely the frequencies of the less common alleles, using R 2 R^{2} and MAE. Population structure is assessed by projection into reference genotype-PC space. Generated NN IBS similarity measures within-synthetic nearest-neighbor identity-by-state (IBS) similarity, where lower values suggest more diversity and reduced mode collapse.
